title: The hypertrophy series: sacrificing short term tonnage for long term progress
summary: He refines his tonnage stability idea: tonnage should neither swing wildly nor stay perfectly flat, and short dips are worth it when they buy bigger gains later. Evolving rep ranges are the built-in tool for this: a heavy low-rep set lowers tonnage now but builds the strength for multiple higher-rep sets later. Flexible programs raise tonnage best.
claims: Tonnage should neither roller-coaster nor stay too stable: flat tonnage means you are not progressing and lack control over volume and intensity
A lifter whose tonnage goes up and down but ends higher without injury or tendinitis is better off than one with a slow, perfectly steady climb
Many of his strategies are long-term investments; a newly added lift starts light and costs tonnage, but later accumulates more and adds flexibility
Do not apply tonnage sacrifices everywhere or you get roller-coaster volume; confine them to select, compartmentalised parts of the program
Evolving rep ranges are engineered for this; going from one heavy set of 4 squats to three sets of 6-8 makes tonnage swing hugely
The single high-intensity low-rep set builds strength until the weight you did for 4 becomes one you can do for 6-7 over multiple sets: tonnage sacrificed now returns later
Program flexibility is directly correlated with your ability to increase tonnage; evolving rep ranges everywhere add flexibility but demand more tracking
Within a body part split, evolving rep ranges let tonnage rise not just overall but for the right muscle groups, as stably and optimally as possible
